lessons.title: Saying when: time, manner, place
lessons.summary: German puts time before place — the exact opposite of English — and chooses between am, im, um and no preposition at all.
lessons.rule:
A German sentence has one hard rule you already know: the verb sits in second position. Everything else — when, why, how, where — comes after it, and it comes in a fixed order. That order is this whole lesson. Germans remember it as TeKaMoLo:

  • Te = temporal — when? morgen, um acht Uhr, jeden Tag
  • Ka = kausal — why? wegen der Arbeit
  • Mo = modal — how? mit dem Zug, zu Fuß, allein
  • Lo = lokal — where? nach Berlin, ins Büro

So: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin. — when, how, where. English says exactly the same thing in almost the opposite order: I'm going to Berlin by train tomorrow — where, how, when. That reversal is why the time keeps sliding to the end of your German sentences for months. Burn in the short version: time first, place last. You will rarely need all four slots at once — two is normal, three is a long sentence.

You can also lift the time expression to the very front, and Germans do this constantly: Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin. But the verb still has to be the second element, so the subject jumps behind it. Morgen fahre ich — never Morgen ich fahre. The rest of the order (how, then where) stays exactly as it was.

Which little word goes in front of the time? Three of them cover nearly everything. um for clock times: um 8 Uhr. am for days, dates and parts of the day: am Montag, am Wochenende, am Abend, am 3. Mai. im for months and seasons: im Januar, im Sommer. One oddity to memorise on its own: it is in der Nacht, not am.

And sometimes you use no preposition at all. Anything built with next, last or every stands completely bare: nächste Woche, letzten Monat, jeden Tag, jeden Morgen. So do heute, morgen and gestern. Turkish marks this with an ending and English adds on or in, so your instinct will be to put something there. Resist it — in nächster Woche is wrong, it is simply nächste Woche.

tables.title: TeKaMoLo — the order of everything after the verb
One sentence, filled slot by slot
am / im / um / nothing
rows: days, dates, parts of the day
am Montag, am Abend, am 3. Mai

examples.de: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin.
examples.en: I'm going to Berlin by train tomorrow.
examples.note: When (morgen), how (mit dem Zug), where (nach Berlin) — the English sentence lists them backwards.

examples.de: Wir treffen uns um acht Uhr vor dem Kino.
examples.en: We're meeting at eight in front of the cinema.
examples.note: Time before place. Putting vor dem Kino first would sound wrong to a German ear.

examples.de: Sie fährt jeden Tag mit dem Fahrrad zur Arbeit.
examples.en: She rides her bike to work every day.
examples.note: jeden Tag takes no preposition, and it still comes before how and where.
Time moved to the front, so the verb stays second and ich lands behind it.

examples.de: Im Januar bin ich nicht hier.
examples.note: Months take im — and again, fronting the time pushes the subject after the verb.

examples.de: Ich gehe am Montag zum Arzt.
examples.en: I'm going to the doctor on Monday.
examples.note: Days of the week take am, never um.

mistakes.why: This is the number one word-order error, straight out of English. German is time first, place last — always.

mistakes.wrong: Ich gehe um Montag ins Kino.
mistakes.right: Ich gehe am Montag ins Kino.
mistakes.why: um is only for the clock. Days of the week and parts of the day take am.

mistakes.wrong: Ich fahre in nächster Woche nach Hamburg.
mistakes.right: Ich fahre nächste Woche nach Hamburg.
mistakes.why: Time phrases with nächste, letzte or jeden take no preposition at all. Adding one is a real overcorrection learners make.
Fronting the time does not buy you an extra slot. The verb must still be the second element, so the subject moves behind it.

drills.question: Ich gehe ___ Montag ins Kino.
drills.explain: Days of the week always take am, even though English says on.

drills.question: Der Film beginnt ___ 20 Uhr.
drills.explain: um is reserved for an exact time on the clock.

drills.question: ___ Januar fahre ich nach Wien. (in January)
drills.explain: Months take im, and putting it first is fine because the verb still follows in second place.

drills.question: Which sentence is correct?
drills.explain: Time comes before place, and the verb has to stay in second position.

drills.question: Ich gehe ___ Tag zu Fuß zur Arbeit. (every)
drills.explain: jeden Tag needs no preposition in front of it — the bare phrase is already complete.

drills.answer: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin
drills.explain: When, then how, then where — the reverse of the English sentence.
The time expression takes first place, so the subject has to slide behind the verb.

drills.answer: Wir treffen uns um acht Uhr vor dem Kino
drills.explain: The clock time comes before the place, and clock times take um.

lessons.title: Numbers, telling the time, and dates
lessons.summary: German says numbers backwards above twenty, uses the 24-hour clock officially, and halb drei means 2:30 — not 3:30.
lessons.rule:
Up to twelve you simply memorise: null, eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn, elf, zwölf. From 13 to 19 you glue the digit onto zehn: dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn — but sechzehn and siebzehn quietly drop a letter, and so do sechzig and siebzig.

Then German goes backwards. From 21 upwards the small digit is said first, joined by und, and the whole thing is written as one word: einundzwanzig is literally one-and-twenty. 47 is siebenundvierzig — seven-and-forty. Hundreds go in front as normal: 134 is hundertvierunddreißig.

This is not a cute quirk, it is a daily problem. Someone reads you a phone number or an account number and you write 72 where they said 27, because the zwei arrived first. Prices too: 3,50 € is said drei Euro fünfzig — and note the comma. German uses a comma where English uses a decimal point, and a dot where English uses a thousands comma, so 1.500 means one thousand five hundred.

The clock. Timetables, appointments, opening hours and anything official use the 24-hour clock: Der Zug fährt um 14:32 Uhr, spoken vierzehn Uhr zweiunddreißig. In casual speech people use 1 to 12 — and here is the trap that catches everyone: halb drei means 2:30, not 3:30. German halb looks forward: half-way to three. So 7:30 is halb acht. The rule of thumb is add one to the English hour.

The rest is friendly: Viertel nach drei is 3:15, Viertel vor drei is 2:45, zehn nach vier is 4:10, zwanzig vor fünf is 4:40. (In eastern and southern Germany you will also hear viertel drei for 2:15 — just know it exists.) Dates run day.month.year: 03.08.2026 is 3 August 2026, so an American-style 08.03 would be read as 8 March. The dot after a number means 3rd, and am 3. Mai is spoken am dritten Mai.

examples.note: One-and-thirty, written as a single word with no spaces.

examples.de: Der Zug fährt um halb drei.
examples.note: halb drei is half-way to three, so it is 2:30 — not 3:30.
7:45. vor means before, so a quarter of an hour is still missing.
Written 3,50 € — the comma is the decimal point in German.
Spoken sechzehn Uhr zwanzig. Timetables are always 24-hour.
Day first, then month, then year.

mistakes.wrong: Es ist halb drei. — I understand: 3:30
mistakes.right: Es ist halb drei. — It is 2:30.
mistakes.why: German halb points forward to the hour it names. For 3:30 you say halb vier.
The small digit comes first, joined by und, and the whole number is one written word.
German dates are day.month.year. Writing it the American way puts you in the wrong month on real forms.

mistakes.wrong: Das kostet drei Punkt fünfzig Euro.
mistakes.why: German writes 3,50 € with a comma and says the cents as a plain number after the euros.

drills.question: 21 heißt auf Deutsch ___
drills.explain: German names the single digit first and joins it to the ten with und.

drills.question: Schreib die Zahl als Wort: 45 = ___
drills.explain: Five-and-forty, in that order and as one word with no spaces.

drills.question: Es ist halb drei. Wie spät ist es?
drills.explain: halb counts towards the hour that is named, so it is thirty minutes before three.

drills.question: Es ist Viertel vor sechs. Wie spät ist es?
drills.explain: vor means before, so a quarter of an hour is still missing until six.

drills.question: 15:15 sagt man: Viertel ___ drei. (nach oder vor)
drills.explain: The quarter hour has already passed three o'clock, so it is nach.

drills.question: Das Datum 03.08.2026 ist der ___. August 2026.
drills.explain: German dates put the day before the month, so 03 is the day.

drills.answer: Der Zug fährt um halb acht
drills.explain: Clock times take um, and halb acht is 7:30.
Age uses the plain number, and 31 is one-and-thirty in German.

lessons.title: es gibt and man — two phrases you need constantly
lessons.summary: es gibt means there is / there are and always takes the accusative; man means people in general and takes the er/sie/es verb form.
lessons.rule:
es gibt is how German says there is and there are. Word for word it means it gives, which is useless as a translation — so learn it as one frozen block and stop taking it apart.

Two facts about it, and neither ever changes. First, the form is always es gibt, even when you are talking about a hundred things. Es gibt einen Supermarkt. Es gibt viele Leute. Never es geben, never sie gibt — the subject of the sentence is that little es, not the things that exist.

Second, what follows it is in the accusative. The accusative is the form a noun takes when it is the thing a verb acts on — I see the man, I buy a coffee. In practice only masculine words visibly change, and they change like this: ein → einen, der → den, kein → keinen. So Es gibt einen Supermarkt, but Es gibt eine Apotheke (feminine) and Es gibt ein Problem (neuter) with no change at all. Questions behave the same: Gibt es hier einen Bahnhof?

The second phrase is man. It means one / you / people in general — nobody specific. English has one, but it sounds so formal that people avoid it; German man is completely ordinary and you will meet it every day, above all in rules and on signs: Hier darf man nicht parken. Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch? In Deutschland bezahlt man oft bar.

Two things to keep straight. man always takes the same verb form as er/sie/es: man sagt, man kann, man darf — never man sagen. And man (one n, small m) is not der Mann (two n, capital M, an adult male). They sound identical out loud, so only context tells them apart — but in writing the difference is visible and getting it wrong is noticed.

tables.title: es gibt is always followed by the accusative
man takes the er/sie/es verb form

examples.note: Masculine ein turns into einen because everything after es gibt is accusative.

examples.de: Es gibt viele Leute im Park.
examples.en: There are a lot of people in the park.
examples.note: English switches to there are; German keeps es gibt unchanged.
kein follows the same pattern as ein, so masculine Kaffee gives keinen.

examples.de: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
examples.en: How do you say that in German?
examples.note: Probably the most useful sentence in your first month — and it uses man, not du.

examples.en: You're not allowed to park here.
examples.note: Exactly what the sign means. man is how rules are written in German.

examples.de: In Deutschland bezahlt man oft bar.
examples.en: In Germany people often pay cash.
examples.note: The place comes first, so the verb stays second and man follows it.

mistakes.why: Everything after es gibt is accusative, and masculine ein becomes einen there. This is the single most common es gibt error.
The subject is es, not the people, so the verb never becomes plural. es gibt never changes shape.
man feels like it means many people, but grammatically it is a single he/she/it. Verb form: darf.

mistakes.wrong: Wie sagt Mann das auf Deutsch?
mistakes.right: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
mistakes.why: Mann with two n and a capital M is an adult male. The general word is man — one n, lowercase.

drills.question: Gibt es hier ___ Supermarkt?
drills.explain: es gibt is always followed by the accusative, where masculine ein becomes einen.

drills.question: Es ___ viele Restaurants in der Stadt.
drills.explain: es gibt keeps its singular form even when the thing that exists is plural.

drills.question: Es gibt ___ Apotheke in der Nähe. (a — die Apotheke)
drills.explain: Feminine eine looks identical in the accusative, so nothing changes here.

drills.question: Wie ___ man das auf Deutsch?
drills.explain: man always takes the same verb form as er, sie or es.

drills.question: Hier darf ___ nicht parken. (people in general)
drills.explain: German uses man wherever English says a general you in a rule.

drills.question: Which sentence is correct?
drills.explain: Problem is neuter (das Problem), and neuter ein does not change in the accusative.
kein takes the same accusative endings as ein, so masculine Kaffee becomes keinen.
hier takes first place, so the verb stays second and man moves behind it.
